c.text: Chapter 5 – Keeping Your Team
Recruiting is the easy part
A ministry can appear to have a recruitment problem when it also needs to address retention. Before making another appeal, ask what serving on the team has been like.

People say yes, serve for a few months, drift to the back of the rota, and then quietly stop. Nobody has a conversation about it. The leader concludes the church is uncommitted and starts asking for volunteers again.
People leave for many reasons, including work, health, caring responsibilities, a move or a change of calling. Three preventable problems also deserve your attention:
They never knew exactly what was expected, so they lived with a low hum of feeling they were doing it wrong.
Nobody ever said thank you in a way that landed.
They could not tell whether their presence made any difference.
They stopped growing.
Year three looked exactly like year one, and nobody ever asked what they wanted to become.
You can do something about all three, while recognising that a healthy team still has people who need to leave.
Jesus trained by sending, then debriefing

Mark 6:7 says Jesus called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits. He did not send them alone, and he did not send them empty-handed. Matthew 10 records the instructions he gave first – where to go, what to say, what to take, what to do when a town would not receive them. Concrete briefing before deployment.
Then Mark 6:30 records what happened when they came back: the apostles gathered around Jesus and reported to him all they had done and taught.
That is the pattern. Brief, send in pairs, debrief.

Luke 10:1-20 shows the same shape at a larger scale with the seventy-two, and adds something important. They come back thrilled that even the demons submitted to them. Jesus does not dismiss the joy, but he redirects it in verse 20 – do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
He debriefed the people, not just the results. He was interested in what serving was doing to them.
Most of us send volunteers out with a vague description and never ask how it went. Then we wonder why they fade.
The training sequence that actually transfers a skill

Ephesians 4:11-12 describes Christ giving leaders to equip his people for service and build up the body. The emphasis is on preparing people to participate, rather than keeping ministry in the hands of a few.
Your job includes helping people develop the understanding, confidence and skills to serve well.
The sequence is four steps, and skipping any of them is why delegation fails:

1. I do it, you watch. Explain what you are doing as you go, including the small judgement calls. 2. We do it together. They take part, you are beside them. 3. You do it, I watch. They lead, you say nothing unless something is going badly wrong. Feedback afterwards, privately. 4. You do it, I’m available. You step out. You are reachable, but you are not standing there. Most leaders jump from step one to step four and call it delegation. The person then fails, the leader takes the job back, and both of them conclude the volunteer wasn’t up to it.
Delegate the outcome, not the task
There is a difference between “put out forty chairs in six rows” and “make sure the room is ready and feels welcoming by 9:30 – here’s what that’s meant to achieve.”
The first produces someone who puts out chairs. The second produces someone who notices the heating is off and fixes it without asking you.
Go back to Jethro in Exodus 18:22: let them judge the ordinary cases themselves, and bring only the hard ones to Moses. Judgement was delegated, not just labour.

When you delegate, agree the outcome, limits and standard first. Allow a different method when it meets those requirements. If work needs correction, explain why and help the person learn. Safety, accuracy and responsible handling of money are not optional standards.
Say thank you like you mean something specific

1 Thessalonians 5:12-13 asks the Thessalonian believers to acknowledge those who work hard among them, and to hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work. Paul thought recognition was worth writing into a letter.
General thanks has a place, but specific appreciation helps people understand the difference their contribution made.

Specific thanks changes people: “I watched you sit with that man for twenty minutes after the service when everyone else had gone. That’s why I asked you to do this.” Name the person, name the action, name why it mattered.
Do it privately and in person as your default.

Do it publicly sometimes, but be careful of always praising the same three people. And thank them in front of their family occasionally. A volunteer’s spouse is carrying the cost of their service and almost never hears about the value of it.
Watch for the weariness before it becomes an exit

Galatians 6:9 urges believers not to become weary in doing good, because at the proper time they will reap a harvest if they do not give up. Paul is writing to a church under pressure, and the word for weary carries the sense of losing heart rather than losing energy.
Excessive hours matter, even when the work is meaningful.
Poor support, unclear expectations and no opportunity to rest can add to the strain. Encouragement should accompany a manageable workload, not compensate for an unsustainable one.
Exodus 17:12 gives the picture I keep coming back to.
During the battle with Amalek, Moses’ hands grew heavy, so Aaron and Hur put a stone under him to sit on and held his hands up, one on each side, until sunset.
Somebody has to hold up the arms of the person holding up the work. In your ministry, that is you – and the people doing it for you are the subject of Chapter 9.
Practically, ask what else each volunteer is carrying.
If someone is caring for a dying parent, offer a lighter load or a break. Do not assume they will ask, and do not make the decision for them without a conversation.
Give people an honest way out
Every role should have a review date – the six-month term from the last chapter. At the review, ask three questions and mean all three:
What part of this do you most enjoy?
What part drains you?
Do you want to continue, change, or stop?
Make “stop” a genuinely acceptable answer.
A volunteer who leaves well after eighteen months, thanked and blessed, tells other people that serving here is a good experience. A volunteer who leaves by disappearing tells them the opposite.
Offer a break if the person wants one.
Agree its length and a review date without promising that a set period will resolve the problem or obliging them to return.
When someone isn’t working out
Sometimes a person is in the wrong role, or is genuinely unsuitable for it. Two principles.
Consider whether a different role would be a better fit.

A capable communicator who struggles with a sound desk may thrive elsewhere. Concerns about abuse, dishonesty or unsafe conduct require the appropriate process; do not transfer a problem to another team. Never let a reliability or attitude problem run for months without a direct conversation. It is unkind to the rest of the team, and it is unkind to the person, who deserves to be told rather than frozen out.

And hold on to John Mark. In Acts 15:37-39 Paul refuses to take him on the second journey because he had deserted them in Pamphylia – the disagreement was sharp enough to split Paul and Barnabas. Barnabas took Mark anyway. Years later, in 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul writes from prison asking Timothy to bring Mark with him, because he is useful to him for ministry.
The volunteer who fails at twenty-two is not finished. Someone had to be Barnabas for that to be true.
